quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Patrick would be ~15 in Thomas Flynn's household; the full household composition would show Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother, if present) and any siblings — currently the mother appears nowhere in the evidence base. The 'United States Census, 1860' collection on FamilySearch is name-searchable (personCount above 0). This is the second-highest priority because it may introduce the mother's name and corroborate or challenge the 1850 co-enumeration inference that is the only current basis for the parent-child link.

Six record types across 10 searches are planned, all on FamilySearch.

Pennsylvania death certificates from this era routinely name both parents including their birthplaces and sometimes nativity parishes, making this the highest-probability single record for directly stating Patrick's parents' names. The 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' collection on FamilySearch is name-searchable (personCount above 0). Search under Flynn and common variants such as Flyn and Flinn.

The 1860 U.S. Federal Census (S2) is already in the project tree as a source for the parent-child relationship R1, but no assertions from it have been extracted for q_001. Patrick would be ~15 in Thomas Flynn's household; the full household composition would show Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother, if present) and any siblings, currently absent from the entire evidence base. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, Register of Wills) is in the project tree as a source for R1 but no assertions from it for q_001 have been extracted. This item's date range is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible death window: born ~1818, he could plausibly have died anywhere from 1860 to 1910, so those years, not Patrick's research window, bound this item, because the record's creator is Thomas. A will naming Patrick as a son is direct evidence of parentage; an intestate administration listing heirs achieves the same. **Survey — what the tree and log already record for this question:**

- 1850 census (src_001): Patrick, age ~5, in the Schuylkill County household of Thomas Flynn (head) — inferred co-residence, no stated relationship column
- 1860 census (src_003): Patrick Flynn, age 15, again in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household — inferred from household position and shared surname
- 1908 death certificate (src_004): names Thomas Flynn as father; informant was son-in-law James Brown (secondary information, family not present at birth; also conflicts with census birthplace — cert says Pennsylvania, censuses say Ireland)
- Patrick's mother is unnamed in every source held

**Active plan pl_002 — item status:**

- pli_004 (census, 1860, FamilySearch) — completed
- pli_005 (vital record / death cert, 1908, FamilySearch) — completed
- pli_006 (probate, Schuylkill County, 1870-1890, FamilySearch) — in_progress, no log entry

**pli_006 is the next step.** The `collections_search` this session confirms the available collection is "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196), which returned `personCount: 0` — this is browse-only (personCount 0). The search is an image browse of Schuylkill County's probate dockets for Thomas Flynn, not a name search. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence and would also likely name Thomas's wife, supplying Patrick's mother.

After pli_006 closes, pl_002's items would all be `completed`/`skipped`, and the plan could move to `completed` to clear the way for a new round. The delegation requests a fresh plan targeting church and probate records — the `collections_search` also returned "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records," name-searchable, covering 1708–1985 — those are the collections a next-round plan would draw on.

**However, a new plan cannot be written yet for two reasons:**

1. pli_006 is still `in_progress` and must close before pl_002 can complete and a new `active` plan can be created.
2. The `localities` section holds no entry for Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. A new plan requires the know-how from a locality survey (jurisdictional history, record survival, boundary quirks). When pli_006 closes, the orchestrator must run `locality-guide` for Schuylkill County before re-invoking research-plan.

**Hand-back:** Route pli_006 to **search-records** (FamilySearch, browse-only image search of Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994, Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County, 1870-1890). Once that closes, the orchestrator should run `locality-guide` for Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, then re-invoke research-plan for the fresh plan.

---

The question of Patrick Flynn's parentage is one step away from completing this plan round. The one remaining item is a browse through Schuylkill County's probate dockets on FamilySearch — a will or estate file for Thomas Flynn, filed roughly between 1870 and 1890, would be the strongest direct evidence available, potentially naming Patrick as a son and also revealing Patrick's mother's name, which no record found so far has supplied. The collection is images only, not name-indexed, so the search is a hands-on browse rather than a quick lookup.

Once that search finishes, the orchestrator will run a locality survey for Schuylkill County to gather the jurisdictional and record-survival details needed to scope the next round, then return here to write the church-and-probate plan the delegation is expecting.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

The Irish surname 'Sheahan' strongly suggests a Roman Catholic background. Parish records — membership transfers from a prior parish, marriage or burial entries stating age and birthplace — could document when Michael first appears in a Schuylkill County parish and what his stated origin was. A transfer record in particular would carry the name of the parish he transferred from, directly showing his prior location. Under loc_001, these parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1961. If Michael Sheahan was Irish-born — consistent with his surname — naturalization papers filed in Schuylkill County could name his birth country, date and port of U.S. arrival, his prior U.S. residence (bearing directly on whether he relocated from another Pennsylvania county or arrived directly in Schuylkill), and his occupation at the time of filing. Patrick Sheahan's 1875 land purchase (Deed Book 42, p. 118 — already in the tree as source S2) is in this same record series. Michael may also appear as a grantee, grantor, or witness in deeds from 1882 onward; a deed entry would establish his arrival in the county independently of the census and might name a mining company or colliery as grantor for a leased lot. As loc_001 notes, coal-region laborers often leased rather than purchased outright, so a lease agreement in the deed books would be equally useful. The 1900 census included a column for year of immigration, which would confirm whether Michael was foreign-born and when he arrived in the United States — bearing directly on whether economic conditions in Ireland or opportunity in the Pennsylvania coal region drove his relocation. The census would also show his occupation 18 years after the 1882 arrival, confirming whether coal mining was sustained. The United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. Search 'Sheahan' and variants within Schuylkill County; also search Patrick Sheahan as a FAN check to corroborate the household context.

Coal company employment ledgers, colliery payroll books, and mine inspector reports for the anthracite coal region of Schuylkill County are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and the Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton). If Michael can be identified in a named colliery ledger, such a record would directly confirm which mine employed him upon his 1882 arrival, the hire date, and sometimes the recruit's prior location. None of these series appeared in the FamilySearch collections_search or volume_search results; they require correspondence with the archives or an on-site visit. This item should be pursued if the census and church items (sequence 1-5) fail to establish the specific mine or the reason for the move beyond occupation.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

If Patrick Flynn (born ~1845, age ~35 in 1880) still resided with Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, age ~62), the relationship would be directly stated as son/father — upgrading the two prior indirect co-residence entries to a near-direct statement of parentage. Also searches for Thomas Flynn heading his own household to catch Patrick recorded separately, and for any widow of Thomas Flynn, which would introduce Patrick's mother for the first time. Variant spellings (Flyn, Flinn, Flyyn) should be tried if the primary spelling yields nothing. Searches both Thomas and Patrick as principals.

The 1870 census (FamilySearch collection 1438024, name-searchable) fills the gap between the already-searched 1860 result and the 1880 search above. Patrick would be ~25 and Thomas ~52 — Thomas is likely still alive and heading his own household. Like 1860, no relationship column, but continued co-residence with shared surname in the same county strengthens the chain of indirect parentage evidence. Critically, a wife of Thomas would appear in this household, naming Patrick's mother for the first time. Variant spellings should be tried. Searches both Thomas and Patrick as principals.

Required parentage plan item: a dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to his wife — the record that identifies Patrick's mother. The loc_001 locality entry notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; sacramental registers are held at the parish and diocese level. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) covers 1708–1985. Thomas was born ~1818 and Patrick ~1845, so the marriage most likely fell in the range 1835–1852. The marriage record would supply the mother's maiden name — which neither census enumeration nor the death certificate recorded — and would corroborate Thomas as Patrick's father by placing the couple as a unit before Patrick's birth. Note the limit: the marriage record establishes Thomas and his wife as a couple; it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child — that link relies on the co-residence census evidence already extracted. Date range is bounded by Thomas's plausible marriageable age (~17) through Patrick's birth year plus a few years' margin.

FAN item (required for a parentage question): search for Patrick Flynn's baptism record and for baptisms of any siblings in the Thomas Flynn family. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) covers the full range. A baptism entry for Patrick would name both parents directly — converting the current indirect census evidence to direct parentage evidence. A sibling's baptism would also name both parents, with the same effect, and would independently corroborate the family unit. Date range extended to 1860 to capture later-born siblings whose records could name both Patrick's father and mother. The loc_001 entry notes that Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese level and some Schuylkill County church films are browse-only image groups — if the name-searchable collection returns no result, volume 007936751 (Church Records, 1842–1895, browse-only) is the next resource.

The proof summary (ps_001) explicitly names Thomas Flynn's probate records as a primary remaining gap. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994' (collection 1999196) and volume 007936749 (Schuylkill County probate, 1851–1930) both have personCount 0 — this is a browse-only (personCount 0) image search of the county dockets at the Register of Wills, not a name search. The loc_001 entry confirms probate records are held by the county Register of Wills and available from 1811. Date range is bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan: born ~1818, he could have died anytime from ~1860 (when Patrick disappears from his household is unknown) to ~1885 (age ~67). The date range is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window. A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of paternity and would very likely advance the conclusion from 'probable' to 'proved'.

The 1900 census (FamilySearch collection 1325221, name-searchable) was identified in the proof summary as a remaining gap. Patrick would be ~55 in 1900 and Thomas (born ~1818, age ~82) almost certainly deceased by then. The search targets Patrick Flynn's own household, which may include a widowed mother living with him — which would introduce Patrick's mother by name and confirm her link to the family for the first time. The 1900 census uniquely records each person's number of years married, number of children born, and number living — details that could help reconstruct the Flynn family structure. The relationship column (present since 1880) would also make any co-residing sibling explicitly labeled. Variant spellings should be tried.

Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 and would have been approximately 16–20 years old during the Civil War (1861–1865), placing him squarely within the service-age window. The FamilySearch collection 'United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861–1865' (collection 1910717, name-searchable) indexes service records. If Patrick served, a compiled service record or pension file would contain biographical data — age, birthplace, and sometimes next-of-kin or family references — that could independently corroborate or expand on his parentage. A pension application in particular often names parents or siblings when establishing dependent relationships. This is a contextual item: a positive result would add supporting evidence; a negative result does not contradict the parentage case.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

output.text_response:
**Plan pl_002** has been created for question q_001 — *Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn?*

---

**What we already know:**
- Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, Ireland; d. 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA)
- Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) appears as head of household in the 1850 and 1860 censuses and is named on Patrick's death certificate — strong indirect evidence he is Patrick's father
- Patrick's **mother is entirely unknown**
- Only the 1850 census has been extracted for this question so far

---

**Research Plan — 10 items in execution order:**

| # | ID | Record Type | Source / Collection | Notes |
|---|-----|------------|---------------------|-------|
| 1 | pli_004 | Census | 1860 US Census (FS 1473181) | Thomas's household — first chance to name Patrick's mother |
| 2 | pli_005 | Census | 1870 US Census (FS 1438024) | Tracks Thomas (~52) with wife & birthplace |
| 3 | pli_006 | Census | 1880 US Census (FS 1417683) | First census to record relationship to head; lists parents' birthplace countries |
| 4 | pli_007 | Census | 1900 US Census (FS 1325221) | Both parents' birthplace countries; within Patrick's lifetime |
| 5 | pli_008 | Church | PA Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) | Baptisms of PA-born siblings would name both parents |
| 6 | pli_009 | Church | Thomas Flynn's marriage (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1840–1870) | Best chance to recover mother's maiden name |
| 7 | pli_010 | Church | Browse-only microfilm vol. 007936751 (1842–1895) | Fallback for pli_008 if indexed search yields nothing |
| 8 | pli_011 | Probate | Schuylkill Co. Probate, col. 1999196 (1851–1930) | Thomas's will would directly name Patrick as son; admin would name the widow |
| 9 | pli_012 | Vital Record | PA Marriage Licenses, vol. 007936753 (1870–1910) | Patrick's own marriage — often names groom's father (and sometimes mother) |
| 10 | pli_013 | Military | Civil War Soldiers Index (FS 1910717, 1861–1865) | If Patrick served, pension file names parents, birthplace, next of kin |

---

**Important note:** Assertions from Patrick's 1908 death certificate (S3) for q_001 have **not yet been extracted** — that extraction should be done alongside these searches, as the death certificate may already name both parents.

**Ready to begin?** The recommended first step is **pli_004** — searching the 1860 US Census for Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Shall I proceed with that search?

openQuestions.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: The 1860 US Federal Census (collection 1473181, name-searchable) is the next surviving census after 1850. Thomas Flynn (I2) is already cited in the project tree as Patrick's father via S2 (1860 Census, Schuylkill Co., dwelling 112, quality 2), but no assertions from S2 have been extracted for q_001. Searching the household will confirm Thomas Flynn's presence, name his wife — Patrick's probable mother — and list siblings, all of whom are unknown to the project. Search under 'Thomas Flynn' and variant 'Thomas Flinn' in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

The 1870 US Federal Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) shows Thomas Flynn (~age 52) in his Schuylkill County household ten years after 1860, naming his wife with her age and birthplace. Patrick (~age 25) may appear in the same household or an adjacent one. This census captures the household at a period when Thomas was still working-age and Patrick was a young adult, cross-checking continuity with the 1860 and 1880 entries. Search under 'Thomas Flynn' and 'Thomas Flinn' in Schuylkill County.

The 1880 US Federal Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) was the first to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. Thomas Flynn (~age 62) should appear in Schuylkill County; his wife and any co-resident children would be labeled 'wife' and 'son/daughter,' giving the clearest census evidence of parentage and the mother's given name. Patrick (~age 35) may appear in the same household or his own nearby. Also states each person's father's and mother's birthplace. Search under 'Thomas Flynn,' 'Patrick Flynn,' and their Flinn variants.

The 1900 US Federal Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) records exact birth month and year and the birthplace of each person's father and mother. Patrick Flynn (~age 55) should appear in Schuylkill County; Thomas Flynn (~age 82) may still be alive. Even if Thomas has died, Patrick's 1900 entry states both parents' birthplace countries and, if he was head of household, his wife's name. This census spans the later part of the question's window (after Patrick's likely marriage and before his 1908 death).

The loc_001 locality entry confirms Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese level. FamilySearch collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records, name-searchable) covers 1708-1985 and includes baptisms, confirmations, and marriages. Patrick was born in Ireland (~1845), so his own baptism is not in a Pennsylvania register; however, any siblings born in Schuylkill County after the family's immigration would have Pennsylvania baptisms naming both Thomas and his wife (the mother). Search under 'Flynn' and 'Flinn' for baptisms of children of Thomas Flynn.

A dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother — a required item for any parentage plan. Thomas Flynn (I2, born ~1818 Ireland) married his wife before or around the time the family emigrated; if the marriage took place in Schuylkill County, it would appear in FamilySearch collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (name-searchable). The marriage record confirms the couple as a unit and supplies the mother's maiden name, which censuses and probate records typically omit. The civil Schuylkill County marriage volume (image group 007936753) covers only 1870-1910 and is too late for Thomas's first marriage. Note: the surname this record gives the mother may be a prior married name rather than her birth surname if she was previously married; corroborate before treating it as her maiden name. A negative result here establishes that Thomas's marriage is not in Pennsylvania records and directs research toward Irish origins.

Image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895, browse-only (personCount 0)) is the digitized microfilm underlying the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH indexed collection. If items 5 and 6 yield nothing from the name-searchable collection, this volume must be browsed image by image for Flynn and Flinn baptism and marriage entries. The loc_001 locality entry notes that some anthracite-region church films are browse-only with approximately 0% record-searchable, confirming that the indexed collection may not reflect the full contents of this film.

The loc_001 locality entry confirms Schuylkill County probate records (wills and administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994, browse-only (personCount 0)) covers Schuylkill County; image group 007936749 (Probate Records, 1851-1930) is the digitized docket. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already listed in the project's source descriptions but has no assertions extracted for q_001, indicating it has not yet been searched. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) would plausibly have died between 1858 and 1910; the date window is set to his plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window. A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence; an intestate administration naming his widow would supply the mother's name and confirm the family unit. Browse the docket register under 'Flynn' and 'Flinn'.

FAN-directed item: Patrick Flynn's own marriage record contains evidence about his parents. Pennsylvania marriage bonds and licenses from this period frequently name the groom's father and sometimes his mother. FamilySearch image group 007936753 (Schuylkill County Marriage Records, 1870-1910, browse-only (personCount 0)) covers the most likely window for Patrick's marriage (~age 20-63). A marriage record naming Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father would corroborate the census co-enumeration evidence; naming Patrick's mother by name would be new information not yet in the project. Date range bounded by Patrick's earliest plausible adult years and his 1908 death. Search under 'Patrick Flynn' and 'Patrick Flinn'.

Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) would have been 16-20 during the Civil War (1861-1865) — within the typical enlistment age range. FamilySearch collection 1910717 (United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865, name-searchable) is the discovery step. If Patrick appears, a pension application file (held at NARA) frequently names a soldier's parents, birthplace town, and next of kin, providing direct parentage evidence. Search under 'Patrick Flynn' and 'Patrick Flinn' in Pennsylvania. A negative result here confirms Patrick did not serve in a Pennsylvania regiment under either spelling.

agent_returns.text:
Plan pl_002 is written and valid. Here is the full return.

**Mode:** Create (first plan for q_001)
**Question:** q_001 — "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Step 1 survey — what the tree already records:**

- Patrick Flynn (I1), fact F1: birth ~1845, place Ireland (sourced to S1 — 1850 Census, Schuylkill Co., dwelling 84). Note: the project objective states "born ca. 1845 in Pennsylvania" but the tree's recorded birthplace is Ireland.
- Patrick Flynn (I1), fact F2: death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (sourced to S3 — death cert no. 4521).
- Thomas Flynn (I2), fact F3: birth ~1818, Ireland (unsourced in the tree).
- Relationship R1: Thomas Flynn (I2) as parent of Patrick (I1), quality 2 on all three sources — S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 Census, dwelling 112), S3 (death cert no. 4521). All three sources support the relationship but no assertions from S2 or S3 have been extracted for q_001.
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is listed in the tree's source descriptions but is not cited by any fact, relationship, or assertion and has not been searched.
- Assertions a_004 and a_005: both extracted from S1 (1850 census) only; a_004 records Patrick as listed in Thomas Flynn's household (indirect evidence, record_basis: inferred); a_005 records Thomas Flynn as head of household.
- Proof summary ps_001: tier "possible," shortfall "gap." Narrative states only the 1850 census has been searched; post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records not yet searched; mother completely unknown.
- No plan items previously existed for q_001 (log count: 0; plans for q_001 count: 0 prior to this call).

**Plan pl_002 — items in execution order:**

- pli_004 | census | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | 1860 US Census (collection 1473181, name-searchable) — S2 is already in the tree citing this census for R1 but no assertions extracted for q_001; full-household search names Thomas's wife (Patrick's unknown mother) and siblings
- pli_005 | census | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | 1870 US Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) — tracks Thomas Flynn (~52) with wife and birthplace data ten years on
- pli_006 | census | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | 1880 US Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) — first census to record relationship to head of household explicitly; also records each person's father's and mother's birthplace
- pli_007 | census | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) — records both parents' birthplace countries; spans the later part of the question's window before Patrick's 1908 death
- pli_008 | church | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (name-searchable, 1708-1985) — Pennsylvania siblings baptized after immigration would name Thomas and his wife; Patrick's own baptism is in Ireland
- pli_009 | church | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | Dedicated item: Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, 1840-1870) — supplies the mother's maiden name; the civil marriage volume (007936753) covers only 1870-1910 and is too late for Thomas's first marriage
- pli_010 | church | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | fallback for pli_008 | Church records volume 007936751 (browse-only (personCount 0), 1842-1895) — digitized microfilm underlying SYNTH-PA-CHURCH; browse if items 5 and 6 yield nothing indexed; locality guide confirms anthracite-region films are substantially browse-only
- pli_011 | probate | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | Collection 1999196 / image group 007936749 (browse-only (personCount 0), 1851-1930) — S4 is in the tree sources but never searched; Thomas's will would directly name Patrick as a son; an administration would name the widow; date window set to Thomas's plausible lifespan (~1858-1910)
- pli_012 | vital_record | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | FAN item — Patrick's own marriage record (volume 007936753, browse-only (personCount 0), 1870-1910); Pennsylvania marriage licenses frequently name the groom's father and sometimes his mother; date range 1865-1908
- pli_013 | military | United States | FamilySearch | no fallback | Civil War Soldiers Index (collection 1910717, name-searchable, 1861-1865) — Patrick (~16-20 during the war) may have served; a subsequent pension file at NARA names parents, birthplace and next of kin

**Baptism note:** Patrick was born in Ireland (~1845), predating any Schuylkill County register. His 1908 death certificate (S3, already in the tree) may name both parents — assertions from S3 for q_001 have not yet been extracted. That extraction is an extraction agent task, not a plan search item, and should be actioned alongside this plan.

**Total scope:** 10 searches, all on FamilySearch (6 name-searchable, 4 browse-only image browse). No items require an external paid repository at this stage.

**Hand-back:** All items are on FamilySearch. The delegation did not authorize execution, so this is handed to **search-records** to execute. Start with pli_004 (1860 census) — would you like to begin?

This plan is for identifying the parents of Patrick Flynn, an Irish immigrant who was living in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania by 1850 and died there in 1908. We already know Thomas Flynn appears in Patrick's household in both the 1850 and 1860 census records and is named on Patrick's death certificate, but those records have only been partly analyzed and Patrick's mother is entirely unknown. The plan works through the most informative sources in order: the 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses (each progressively more explicit about family relationships and parents' origins), then Catholic church records in Schuylkill County that may record baptisms of Patrick's Pennsylvania-born siblings naming both parents, a dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother (the one record most likely to give her maiden name), a browse of unindexed church microfilm if the indexed search turns up nothing, Thomas Flynn's probate file (a will would directly name Patrick as a son and name the widow), Patrick's own marriage record (which under Pennsylvania practice often names the groom's father), and finally the Civil War soldiers index to check whether Patrick served, since a pension file would name his parents and birthplace.

The first step is to search the 1860 federal census for Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household, which is expected to name his wife for the first time.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
